triage.name: Acute prostatitis
triage.reason: Fever, dysuria, perineal pain and tender prostate on exam; diagnosed clinically with urine testing, with a clear differential.

demographics: Occurs in males of all ages; most common in sexually active adult men

risk_factors.text: Indwelling urinary catheter or recent instrumentation of the urinary tract
Benign prostatic hyperplasia or other bladder outlet obstruction
Recent prostate biopsy or transurethral procedure

chief_complaints.text: I have to pee all the time
The area between my scrotum and anus hurts
I have a fever and feel awful

hpi.onset: Fairly abrupt, developing over hours to a day or two
hpi.duration: Usually a few days at presentation
hpi.progression: Rapidly worsening urinary burning and frequency with increasing perineal and pelvic pain, often accompanied by fever and chills
hpi.location: Perineum, suprapubic region, and sometimes the lower back or rectum
hpi.radiation: May radiate to the lower back, groin, or penis
hpi.quality: Burning with urination; deep, aching, or pressure-like pain in the perineum and pelvis
hpi.severity: Moderate to severe; often 6–8/10 at presentation
hpi.timing: Constant, worse with urination and with bowel movements

associated_symptoms.text: Feeling like the bladder isn't empty after urinating

pertinent_negatives: Flank pain radiating to the groin in waves
Prior similar episodes with no fever

positives.text: Feeling like the bladder isn't empty after urinating

argues_against: Colicky flank pain radiating to the groin
Severe back pain with neurologic deficits

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with confusion, falls, or generalized weakness rather than classic urinary and perineal symptoms; fever may be blunted.
Symptoms may be milder or more indolent, and fever may be absent despite significant infection; atypical organisms are more likely.
Higher risk of severe infection, abscess formation, and atypical or resistant organisms; presentation may be more severe or masked.
Prepubertal boys are uncommon; when it occurs, they may present with fever, irritability, and nonspecific abdominal or urinary symptoms rather than perineal pain.

general.mild: Uncomfortable but not toxic; able to sit and talk
general.moderate: Ill-appearing, febrile, prefers to shift weight off the perineum
general.severe: Toxic-appearing, flushed, diaphoretic, reluctant to sit still
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, pale, diaphoretic, lethargic or confused

findings.maneuver: Perform a gentle digital rectal exam, palpating the prostate
Palpate the prostate during digital rectal exam
findings.finding: Soft, boggy, enlarged prostate with loss of the normal median sulcus

findings.maneuver: Palpate the perineum between the scrotum and anus
Palpate and percuss the suprapubic area for a distended bladder
Palpate the scrotal contents, including the epididymis and testis
Palpate the flanks and abdomen for a mass
Assess for rebound tenderness and rigidity
Inspect the urethral meatus and milk the urethra

labs.caveat: A normal white count does not exclude acute prostatitis, especially early or in older or immunocompromised patients.
Leukocyte esterase is positive in nearly all patients; a negative result argues against a urinary source.
Positive only with nitrate-reducing organisms such as E. coli; a negative nitrite does not exclude infection.
Supports the diagnosis and helps track response, but is not required.
Higher values suggest bacteremia or a more severe systemic infection.
Rises with dehydration, obstruction, or sepsis; guides antibiotic dosing.
From poor intake, vomiting, or dehydration.
Elevated lactate with hypotension suggests sepsis and warrants urgent resuscitation.
Not applicable in males; listed only because pregnancy must be excluded before pelvic imaging in anyone who could be pregnant.

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Severe illness, suspected abscess, or failure to improve on antibiotics

findings.text: Enlarged, edematous prostate with heterogeneous enhancement

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected prostatic abscess or when CT is unavailable

findings.text: Focal hypoechoic or complex fluid collection suggesting abscess

imaging.study: MRI prostate with and without contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Equivocal CT or ultrasound when abscess is suspected

findings.text: Diffuse prostatic edema with increased T2 signal and restricted diffusion
Usually normal; may show a bladder shadow or calcifications

initial.why: First-line test; pyuria, bacteriuria, and leukocyte esterase support a urinary tract infection
Leukocytosis with left shift supports infection and gauges severity
Assesses hydration, renal function, and electrolytes before antibiotic dosing
Identifies the organism and guides antibiotic choice; obtain before starting antibiotics
Detects bacteremia in febrile or systemically ill patients
initial.only_if: fever, chills, or signs of sepsis

supporting.why: Supports the diagnosis and helps track response to treatment
Suggests bacteremia or severe systemic infection
supporting.only_if: severe illness or concern for sepsis

supporting.why: Screens for sepsis and tissue hypoperfusion

supporting.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
supporting.only_if: severe illness, suspected abscess, or no improvement after 48–72 hours of antibiotics
suspected abscess or CT is unavailable

not_indicated.why: Vigorous prostatic massage is contraindicated in acute prostatitis because of the risk of bacteremia
Not performed during acute infection; risks seeding and bleeding

not_indicated.test: MRI prostate with and without contrast
not_indicated.why: Not routine; reserved for equivocal imaging when abscess is suspected

decision_points: Obtain urine culture before starting antibiotics so susceptibilities are available
Avoid vigorous prostate massage or biopsy during acute infection
If the patient is toxic, hypotensive, or has rigors, treat as sepsis and admit for IV antibiotics
If fever and symptoms do not improve within 48–72 hours of appropriate antibiotics, image for prostatic abscess
Consider sexually transmitted organisms in young sexually active men and adjust coverage accordingly

differential.name: Acute bacterial cystitis
differential.why_considered: Dysuria, frequency, urgency and pyuria are the cardinal features of both, and cystitis is far more common.

history: Suprapubic discomfort only, without perineal or rectal pain
No fever or chills in uncomplicated cases
No pain with ejaculation or bowel movements
exam: Prostate is non-tender and normal on gentle digital rectal exam
labs: Normal or minimally elevated white count

differential.name: Acute epididymitis
differential.why_considered: Scrotal and perineal pain with dysuria and fever in a sexually active man overlaps with prostatitis.

history: Pain localized to the scrotum and radiating along the spermatic cord
exam: Tender, indurated epididymis with a positive Prehn sign
labs: Positive nucleic acid amplification testing for Chlamydia or Gonorrhea in young men
imaging: Scrotal ultrasound showing epididymal enlargement and hyperemia with normal testicular flow

differential.name: Testicular torsion
differential.why_considered: Acute severe scrotal and groin pain with nausea and vomiting can be mistaken for prostatitis when the patient localizes poorly.
differential.trigger: Sudden severe testicular pain with a high-riding, transversely oriented testis and absent cremasteric reflex

history: Abrupt onset, often waking the patient from sleep
imaging: Doppler ultrasound showing absent or reduced testicular blood flow

differential.name: Acute pyelonephritis
differential.why_considered: Fever, chills, dysuria and flank or back pain overlap, and both are ascending urinary infections.

history: Prominent flank pain and high fever with rigors
labs: Pyuria with white blood cell casts
imaging: CT with contrast showing wedge-shaped renal hypodensities or perinephric stranding

differential.name: Prostatic abscess
differential.why_considered: A complication of acute prostatitis that presents identically but fails to improve with appropriate antibiotics.
differential.trigger: Persistent fever and perineal pain after 48–72 hours of appropriate antibiotics

history: Symptoms persist or worsen despite appropriate antibiotics
imaging: CT or transrectal ultrasound showing a rim-enhancing fluid collection within the prostate

differential.name: Chronic prostatitis / chronic pelvic pain syndrome
differential.why_considered: Perineal and pelvic pain with urinary symptoms in a man, but with a very different time course.

history: Symptoms for at least 3 of the past 6 months
exam: Prostate may be tender but is not boggy or acutely inflamed
labs: Urinalysis and urine culture are typically negative

differential.name: Benign prostatic hyperplasia
differential.why_considered: Older men with lower urinary tract symptoms, hesitancy and incomplete emptying may be thought to have infection.

history: Gradual onset over months to years

differential.name: Prostate cancer
differential.why_considered: Can cause perineal or pelvic pain and urinary symptoms, and may be found incidentally during evaluation.

history: No fever or acute systemic illness
Weight loss or bone pain in advanced disease
imaging: MRI showing a focal lesion; biopsy confirms malignancy

severity.mild: Early, uncomplicated: mild dysuria and frequency, low-grade or no fever, no systemic toxicity, able to take oral fluids and antibiotics as an outpatient
severity.moderate: Established infection: fever and chills, significant perineal pain, leukocytosis and pyuria, but hemodynamically stable and able to take oral therapy
severity.severe: Systemically ill: high fever with rigors, toxic appearance, marked leukocytosis, possible acute urinary retention or early sepsis, requiring admission and IV antibiotics
severity.critical: Septic shock or urosepsis from acute prostatitis, with hypotension, tachycardia, altered mental status and organ dysfunction; can be life-threatening

red_flags.meaning: Sepsis or septic shock; needs urgent resuscitation and IV antibiotics
Severe systemic infection or sepsis, especially in older adults

red_flags.finding: Rigors or high fever with toxic appearance
Acute urinary retention or inability to void
red_flags.meaning: Bladder outlet obstruction from prostatic swelling; requires catheterization

red_flags.finding: Persistent fever and pain after 48–72 hours of appropriate antibiotics
red_flags.meaning: Prostatic abscess or resistant organism; image and reassess

red_flags.finding: Flank pain with costovertebral angle tenderness
red_flags.meaning: Concurrent pyelonephritis or upper tract obstruction

complications.name: Chronic prostatitis / chronic pelvic pain syndrome
clues: Persistent perineal pain for months after treatment

special_populations.differences: May present with confusion, falls or generalized weakness rather than classic urinary and perineal symptoms; fever may be blunted, and the prostate may be less tender. Higher risk of retention and sepsis.
Symptoms may be milder or more indolent, fever may be absent despite significant infection, and atypical organisms are more likely. Lower threshold for admission and broad-spectrum antibiotics.
Higher risk of severe infection, abscess formation and atypical or resistant organisms; presentation may be more severe or masked. Tight glucose control is important.
Uncommon in prepubertal boys; when it occurs, they may present with fever, irritability and nonspecific abdominal or urinary symptoms rather than perineal pain. Consider anatomic abnormalities.
Antibiotic doses must be adjusted for renal function; avoid nephrotoxic agents and monitor creatinine closely.

key_questions.question: Where exactly is the pain? Does it hurt between the scrotum and the anus?
key_questions.looking_for: Perineal pain, the feature that separates prostatitis from simple cystitis

key_questions.question: When did this start, and how fast has it gotten worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Abrupt onset over hours to a day or two with rapid worsening, rather than months of gradual symptoms

key_questions.question: Do you have a fever, chills, or shaking rigors?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever and chills suggesting systemic infection; rigors raise concern for bacteremia or sepsis

key_questions.question: Does it burn when you urinate, and are you going more often or feeling an urgent need?
key_questions.looking_for: Dysuria, frequency and urgency, which are almost always present

key_questions.question: Does it hurt to sit, have a bowel movement, or ejaculate?
key_questions.looking_for: Pain with sitting, defecation or ejaculation, which points to the prostate rather than the bladder

key_questions.question: Have you had a urinary catheter, cystoscopy, prostate biopsy, or any recent urinary procedure?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent instrumentation, a strong risk factor and a clue to the likely organism

key_questions.question: Have you had a urinary tract infection recently, or do you have trouble emptying your bladder?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent UTI, benign prostatic hyperplasia or other bladder outlet obstruction

key_questions.question: Are you able to urinate at all right now?
key_questions.looking_for: Acute urinary retention from prostatic swelling, which needs urgent catheterization

key_questions.question: Have you had unprotected sex, including anal intercourse, or new partners?
key_questions.looking_for: Sexually transmitted organisms such as Chlamydia, Gonorrhea or enteric flora

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, HIV, or any condition or medication that weakens your immune system?
key_questions.looking_for: Immunosuppression or diabetes, which raises the risk of severe infection, abscess and atypical organisms

key_questions.question: Any flank pain, nausea or vomiting?
key_questions.looking_for: Flank pain with costovertebral tenderness suggests concurrent pyelonephritis; vomiting suggests systemic illness

key_questions.question: Have you had blood in your urine, or pain in your testicles or scrotum?
key_questions.looking_for: Hematuria is sometimes present; scrotal or testicular pain suggests epididymitis or torsion instead

key_questions.question: Have you had similar episodes of perineal pain lasting months without fever?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic prostatitis or chronic pelvic pain syndrome, which has a very different time course

key_questions.question: Do you have any allergies to antibiotics, especially penicillins or sulfa drugs?
key_questions.looking_for: Allergies that would change the choice of empiric antibiotic

key_questions.question: What medications do you take, including any for the prostate or bladder?
key_questions.looking_for: Alpha-blockers, anticholinergics or recent antibiotics that affect the picture

reasoning_points: Abrupt onset over hours to a day or two of dysuria and frequency with perineal pain
Fever and chills indicating a systemic infection rather than simple cystitis
Exquisitely tender, boggy prostate on gentle digital rectal exam
Pyuria and bacteriuria with leukocyte esterase on urinalysis, and leukocytosis on CBC
Urine culture obtained before antibiotics to identify the organism and guide therapy
Risk factors such as recent instrumentation, catheterization or urinary tract infection
Red flags for sepsis, acute urinary retention or prostatic abscess considered and excluded
Look-alikes such as cystitis, epididymitis, testicular torsion, pyelonephritis and chronic prostatitis distinguished

easy: Sexually active adult man with abrupt dysuria, frequency, fever and perineal pain
Exquisitely tender, boggy prostate on digital rectal exam
medium: Older man with benign prostatic hyperplasia and recent catheterization presenting with fever and urinary symptoms
Young man with a sexually transmitted organism and mild urethral discharge
Concurrent pyelonephritis with flank pain and costovertebral angle tenderness
hard: Older adult presenting with confusion, falls or generalized weakness and a blunted fever
Immunocompromised or diabetic patient with mild symptoms but significant infection or abscess
Patient who fails to improve after 48–72 hours of appropriate antibiotics, suggesting prostatic abscess
Patient in acute urinary retention or early septic shock requiring urgent resuscitation
